faqs.a: Repaying a loan through fixed periodic payments where each payment covers that period's interest and the rest reduces principal. Mortgages, auto loans, and personal loans all amortize this way.
Interest is charged on the full remaining balance, which is largest at the start. As principal shrinks, the interest slice shrinks and the principal slice grows - while your payment stays flat.
faqs.q: Why is my early payment mostly interest?

faqs.a: Extra money goes straight to principal, which jumps you forward in the schedule: every future payment then has a bigger principal slice. Use the Mortgage Payoff Calculator to model it.
faqs.q: How do extra payments affect the schedule?

faqs.a: In the US they usually match (a 30-year term fully amortizes). In Canada, a 25-year amortization is often paid through 5-year terms that renew.
faqs.q: What is the difference between term and amortization?

faqs.a: No - this schedule covers principal and interest only. Add tax, insurance, PMI, and HOA with the Mortgage Calculator for the full monthly picture.
faqs.q: Does this include property tax and insurance?

faqs.a: No. The schedule is computed in your browser.

mortgage-amortization-calculator.formula:
Monthly rate r = annual rate / 12 / 100; n = years x 12
Payment = P x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n)
Each month: interest = balance x r; principal = payment - interest; balance -= principal.
howTo: Enter your loan amount, annual interest rate, and term in years.
Scroll the year-by-year schedule: principal paid, interest paid, remaining balance.
Check total interest to see the true lifetime cost of the loan.
keyFacts: Amortization = paying down a loan with fixed payments that split into interest and principal.
Early payments are mostly interest; late payments are mostly principal - the payment stays the same.
Total interest on a 30-year loan often exceeds half the amount borrowed.
Extra principal payments skip you ahead in the schedule - they do not just shorten the end.
The schedule assumes a fixed rate; adjustable-rate mortgages re-amortize when the rate changes.
Biweekly payments (26 half-payments per year) equal one extra monthly payment yearly.

mortgage-amortization-calculator.workedExample:
$300,000 loan, 6.5% annual rate, 30 years:
1. Monthly rate = 0.541667%, n = 360. Payment = 300,000 x 0.00541667 / (1 - 1.00541667^-360) = $1,896.20.
2. Year 1: principal about $3,353, interest about $19,402, balance $296,647.
3. Total paid = 1,896.20 x 360 = $682,632; total interest = $382,632.
Notice: year-1 interest is almost 6x the principal repaid.
